analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 619, Chester E. Jackson, petitioner, versus John C. Taylor, acting warden, United States Penitentiary. And number 620, Harriel L. Fowler, petitioner, versus Frederick H. Wilkinson, warden, United States Penitentiary of Atlanta, Jordan. Mr. Van Suster. May it please the court? This case is here on writ of certiorari to the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. The case originally arose as a petition for a writ of habeas corpus directed to the warden at the Lewisburg Penitentiary. That petition for a writ of habeas corpus was brought before the District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. On May 7, 1956, the Court of Appeals announced its decision refusing to grant the writ of habeas corpus and free the prisoner. And this court is granted certiorari. The fact of the case is briefly this. The petitioner, Jackson, and another soldier named Fowler, who was a petitioner under case number 620, together with another soldier named D. Custer, were brought to trial before a court-martial that convened in Korea on June 8, 1951. There they were charged in two counts. First, premeditated murder, and second, rape. The court found the defendant, all three of them, in a joint trial, guilty of murder and not guilty of rape, but guilty of attempted rape. Thereupon, the law officer of the court advised the court that the minimum sentence was life imprisonment and the maximum sentence was death. We have no quarrel with the fact that the instruction is given goes outside of the directions contained in the manual for courts-martial. It is only, incidentally, of some importance. The court fixed sentence, life imprisonment. There was no sentence, septic sentence of any kind, for the attempted rape. It was just the one gross sentence. Thereafter, the sentence was, and the findings of guilty, were reviewed by the commanding general, or Korean area, proper person, and they were approved in full, the sentence and the findings of guilty. And thereafter, in routine fashion, it came before the board of review in the office of the judge-advocate general of the army. The board of review found that the record failed to show any evidence that the activity of these three soldiers was in any way connected with the death of the woman. And thereupon it held that the murder charge should be set aside, but the attempted rape charge or conviction was sustained. But instead of setting aside the entire penalty and ordering a new trial, the board of review conceived its authority or its proper function to be that it should make then and there an initial determination of what the sentence should be. The opinion, as it is written, indicates that that board of review felt that it should determine what is an appropriate sentence. But in the order part of the decision, it says that so much of the sentence, as exceeds 20 years, which is the maximum for attempted rape, shall be set aside. It says that so much of the life imprisonment sentence, as exceeds 20 years, is excessive and shall be set aside, and the other 20 years shall be affirmed. Do I understand your only complaint is regarding the impropriety of the sentence? Is that right? Quite that, sir. The complaint is that the board of review had no authority or power to make that sentence. It was limited to authority to return it for rehearing under these circumstances. For rehearing of what? On the proper sentence. On the proper sentence? Yes. That is, the original court-martial would be reconvened for an imposition of sentence. Is that it? The law, the code, the Uniform Code of Military Justice provides that a rehearing shall be conducted before a board composed of officers, not members of the prior. I'm not talking about the board of review, but if you prevail, what would happen? It would be referred for a new trial or a rehearing before a new court-martial with none of the same officers that saturday written. A rehearing of what? The merit? It'd be retrived before the court-martial? No, only as to sentence. With a new court-martial? With a new court-martial. Would you mind telling me what the code provision is as to that? The code provision isn't specific on the subject. It speaks of a rehearing, and then it doesn't refer to what you do when you have a rehearing in a situation such as this, where the penalty has been set aside, the sentence set aside, but the conviction remains. The code is silent. It doesn't fill in there. That's the source, perhaps, of most of our trouble. There is, but a different body of officers would accept the finding of guilt and then determine and have merely a hearing as to what sentence should be imposed. Is that it? I do not wish to say that. The code is silent in situations like this. But at your convention, if you prevail here, what would you be doing? That the board of review will return it for rehearing. I feel that on the rehearing, that the proper thing to do, the only thing to do, is to leave open to the court-martial the function to determine all of the things that happened here, and then permit the court-martial to... But not retry the determination of guilt. No, sir. I don't feel that we can ever claim a right to retrial on the question of guilt. But a different body of officers would assess the heinousness or the gravity of the offense and then decide what sentence is imposed. Correct. That is, as I would interpret, the proper, correct, reasonable application of the code provisions of this situation. Now, the... The... The... It is our contention that, first of all, the code, Article 66, does not grant to the Board of Review the right to make an initial determination of a proper sentence. And secondly, if that article, Article 66, should be so interpreted as to give the Board of Review that authority, then the article in its application to this case would be contrary to the ex post factual provisions of the Constitution. I would like to take up those arguments in that order. First, that they do not have the authority under Article 66. Before you do, did I understand you'd answer, Justice Frankfurter, that you thought there should be a new trial on the merits by a new Board of Officers? A new trial by a whole new court-martial, but I don't feel that we can still have the right to retry the issue of guilt. Just on the question of sentence. Just on the question of sentence. Article 66 is the only part of the code which gives to the Board any authority, whatever, to review cases of this kind. It's the only section. It provides, first of all, that the Board of Review shall act only with respect to findings and sentences as approved by the convening authority. The convening authority being always the general or other officer who appointed the court-martial. I see that it follows that we can read that sentence as this, that it shall act only in respect to sentences which have been imposed by a court-martial, because a convening authority cannot approve any sentence unless it has been approved, unless it has been passed by a court-martial. If we carry on to the next sentence, you find that it is a limiting or negativing sentence. It says that it shall approve only such findings of guilt and the sentence or such part or amount of it as it finds correct in law and in fact and determines on the basis of the entire record to be approved. I contend that the Board of Review has read that clause or that sentence to mean it shall affirm such findings of fact as it remakes or such a sentence as it rebuilds or remakes or redetermines as to be correct. There is no positive language there at all. We come to the next paragraph and it says this. If the Board of Review sets aside the findings and sentence, it may order a rehearing, except under certain circumstances where the setting aside is based on a lack of sufficient evidence in the record, then they may not. But there it is. If the Board sets aside the findings and sentence, it may order a rehearing. If it does not order a rehearing, it shall order that the charges be dismissed. That's the substance of all that the statute, the Code, gives to the Board of Review. The opposition, the respondent, argues perhaps that by implication that authority rests there. Perhaps their strongest argument is that any other system is too difficult to handle. They would quote from us the decisions from the Court of Military Appeals, which says that in the military field or in the military scope, rehearing is impractical if not impossible. That I do not agree with at all. Retrial in the military sphere, especially in time of peace, and this Code was passed during time of peace, is as simple and perhaps easier or simpler than it is in a civilian sphere. The selection of officers is by command, by FIAC, from the general officer. There is no need to call a number of jurors and find excuses who cannot appear. Well, under your proposition, exactly what evidence would be taken? I gather you concede guilt. Now, what would be the evidence that would be heard by the new board? Oh, I believe it would have to hear all of the evidence concerning the facts of the case up to, but not including the fact that the woman died by some method, means, or hand unknown sometime later. Now, how long ago did this incident occur? This occurred in March, on March 16, 1951. Now, that's six years ago. Yes, sir. How practical is a review of the testimony short of the death at this juncture? At this juncture, it is, I think, impractical. But, if it be impractical, that is not the burden or the tough luck of the petitioner. I hold this court upon finding that he is... Well, suppose they can't get a single one of the witnesses at this time. Then what happens? You pleaded guilty. Then what is to follow? Well, I still feel that the court-martial can and may impose sentence because any other interpretation would be so... Well, I know, but I'm trying to get at what's the result of you. What would follow? Suppose they can't, but none of those witnesses are now available, so there can't be any evidence before the new court-martial. I think you have to read from the record of trial in the past. And then impose sentence merely upon what they read. I fear so, but it's in the realm outside of precisely the question necessary here, so I haven't gone into it. My intention is that this man is imprisoned under a void sentence, imposed by a tribunal having no authority to impose that sentence, and therefore, under authority of cases in which is decided by this court, he's entitled to a discharge. The second question of what the Army intends to do will await the Army's actual action in grabbing him and putting him up for new trial. What was the sentence for the attempted rape? Twenty years. Now, supposing the court-martial had said, we'll impose a life sentence on the murder count, we'll impose a twenty-year sentence on the rape count, and, of course, have the two sentences run concurrently. Then, could the Board of Review have said we will take the twenty-year sentence on the rape count? Yes, sir, I don't think there's any doubt about it. What's the difference? Well, you see, the factual situation you proposed takes away all of the sting, all of the unfairness that the present situation involves. Here, we do not know whether the court-martial would have imposed a sentence of five years, or one year, or ten years on that count. And so we contend that such an interpretation as to give to the Board of Review the right to make an initial determination, which is at the same time a final and last determination, is so grossly unfair that the statute should not be interpreted to give to the Board that power by influence. But in these military trials, as I understand it at least, unlike civil cases, criminal cases, civilian cases, the reviewing Board has got a right to review the sentence. To mitigate it? To cut it down? But no one will contend that a reviewing authority has the authority to increase it or to reinstate findings of not guilty, only to cut down, to give clemency, and to remit or set off the excessive portion, which is illegal. But I'd like to suppose a fact like this. Suppose that a court-martial, improperly and erroneously, found him and sentenced the lads to life imprisonment on a murder trial. And then imposed a five-year penalty on the attempted rape charge, both to run concurrently. The concurrent sentence would probably be set aside by the commanding general because it is the Army's idea that the concurrent sentence is improper. I find nothing of that in the code itself as presently enacted, but the uniform unvarying experience for years back has been one gross sentence. The writers, the scholars on military jurisprudence is to the same effect. Now, if the Army had, and if the commanding general had set aside that concurrent sentence, and thereupon, and held to the full life term, thereupon it went to the Board of Review, and the Board of Review then determined that the life sentence is wrong, and it should be reduced to 20 years, which is the maximum for attempted rape, then what? Does the Board have that authority to override the court-martial? What we know the court-martial would do. Surely, I don't think anyone supposes the Court of the Board of Review would have that authority. But if it doesn't have that authority, how can we say that unequivocally and affirmatively the record shows that the Board did not exceed its authority? It might appear argumentatively, inferentially, or in a negative way that the Board did not exceed its authority, but so long as we don't know what the Board of Review would have done to those soldiers, they have not, the record does not show affirmatively and unequivocally, which is the requirement in the Runkle case decided by this court, that the Board in its proceedings conformed to law, or followed the statute after the vote, and that its judgment conformed to law. I would like to take a few minutes now on this question of a violation of the ex post-factual provision of the Constitution. It is our contention that, let me first of all state that the Code of Military Justice, Uniform Code, went into effect on May 31, 1951. That was several weeks or months after the crime committee. The lads were tried on June 8, of 1951, eight days after the effective date. It is our contention that under Article 50 of the prior code, this soldier was required, or this, all three of these soldiers, would have had their cases referred back to the court-martial for a rehearing. If you interpret Article 66 as not doing that, then it means the soldier has only just one chance before the border to do. It makes a determination, it's final and likely. But if you send it under Article 50, send it back to the border, to the court-martial, then the soldier has two additional chances. The court-martial can fix a penalty, and it might be far lower. If he doesn't, the commanding general might reduce it. And if he doesn't, then he still has the border to do as his final chance. Now, this is not merely a matter of procedure. A sentence in the military establishment and the military hierarchy of the tribunals of all three steps is not complete and is not final. It is only interlocutory or inchoate, as one writer has referred to it, until all three of these people have happened. And I contend that it's far more important in the modern day that a soldier or any accused person, let me say this, the question of who is going to determine a sentence where there are maximum and minimum limits is far more important than what are the maximum and minimum limits. If, for example, you can think of permitting the father of the victim of a rape attack to fix the penalty or have any part of determining the penalty, it's far more important to the accused than it is to perhaps raise the maximum and minimum limits by two or three years. Mr. Epstein? Yes, sir. If it please the court, I'll try not to be repetitious, but as we didn't have much time to consolidate our argument, there may be certain repetition in it that has consolidated cases. Well, you represent another defendant anyway, don't you? Yes, sir. I represent the defendant and we came before this court on a little bit different theory of law than did Mr. Van Sesteren. Do you have a separate brief? Yes, sir. It's case number 620. I'd like to go back over the facts just a little bit in this case without going into too much detail and state to the court what actually happened. Fowler, along with defendant DaCosta and defendant Jackson was convicted by a court-martial in Korea. The brief facts of the case which I deem is important is this. Fowler, DaCosta, and Jackson left their post of duty pursuing one of the things a man in the service might want sometime, a little extracurricular activity. In such, they came upon a house in Korea and I believe the court-martial procedure which is part of an exhibit in this court shows that Jackson and DaCosta went into the house and Fowler stayed outside of the house and that Fowler, more or less, his participation in this was as a bystander or as the record says, he stood guard in it. The degree of guilt in the case varied considerably. You said they went into a house. You mean went into someone's home? Yes, sir. Well, you might call it a home. It was outside the evidence. It was more of a shack. Well, it was a habitat for a family anyway. Well, it was a habitat for something. Say pardon? Let's put it was a habitat for something. What do you mean by that? Do you mean that something was secret? I'm getting a little bit outside of the evidence if I do go into that and I didn't care for the court to do it. It was in a district there where there were certain shacks and certain things went on that wouldn't ordinarily go on in a regular neighborhood. Well, are you trying to I don't want to retry the case. The House of Prostitution is distinguished from the home. Yes, sir. Are you that is your point? Yes, sir. I'm trying to infer that. But it's outside of the record and I didn't want to the record doesn't show that and I didn't want to get outside of the record. Well, Fowler stayed outside and these actions took place between DeCosta and Jackson. They during the escapade some Koreans came and ran them off. There was an exchange of fire. The Koreans fired at them. I believe they said they fired back in the air across the creek and ran back to their face. The next morning this woman was found dead. It wasn't shown whether the so-called rescuers killed her whether somebody else killed her or in my mind was never shown conclusively if it was even the same woman. But it was in the same area and the woman who they found according to the medical testimony in the brief in the court-martial had actually been raped. the evidence in the case showed that DaCosta who was the only one that tried to rape her admitted that he tried to have intercourse with her but wasn't able to because of his degree of intoxication. The court-martial was properly convened in the case and all three were convicted of murder including Fowler who stayed on the outside, my client, an attempted rape. Was the woman shot? Is that the way she did it? Yes, so they found a bullet. There was an exchange of fire and they found a bullet wound in her head. That's how she died. Now, I should add here, this wasn't a combat area too where firing would under the circumstances take place. This happened in a combat area. This was in the Korean complex where firing could ordinarily take place through guerrilla activity and others. Now, the court-martial was properly convened and all three were found guilty of murder and attempted rape. The minimum sentence for the murder was life imprisonment. The minimum sentence for attempted rape has no minimum. The maximum was 20 years. And the difficulty in our sentence comes here and now. When these boys were found guilty of the murder, the court-martial lost any discretion as to how much time they could give for attempted rape. If they wanted to on the facts in the attempted rape case, they didn't have to give Fowler anything. They didn't have to give Jackson anything. They didn't have to give DeCosta anything. But because of the finding on the guilty of murder, they had to give all three of them life. The sentence went up to the Board of Review through proper channels. And the Board of Review says there was not enough evidence in the case to show you were guilty of the murder. And saying that, they could have said somebody else killed them. You wasn't even there. All the evidence in this case showed was that you were guilty of attempted rape. then they go to describe the viciousness of the crime and say we deem twenty years an appropriate sentence. Then in their body of opinion they say we remit so much of the life sentence as is in excess of twenty years void. The Army says that's the proper procedure. We say it's not and this is why. the uniform code of military justice as we are not attacking, I'm not, in this particular sense, sets up three steps before a man can be sentenced properly. It says the courts marshal that his case sentences him, which couldn't be done in this case, and they exercise their discretion as to how much time he'll get. Then the convening authority, the commanding general approves it, then it's sent to the board of review for a final determination. Now, if in this case we let the board of review sentence this man, what happens? The board of review has set there as a court-martial on the particular case, and then he's lost two rights of clemency. Number one, the right for the commanding general to say it wasn't that serious, and number two, for somebody to appear before the board of review and try to get the crime lessened. In this particular case, there were certainly degrees of guilt in it. The man that actually commits a crime of attempted rape, and the man that stands guard or stands outside and waits for him, there are certainly degrees of guilt. In this particular case, that could not be shown in any term of the proceeding because the board of review took up a cold record and decided it. Now, the government in their contention says, what's the difference if we send it down to a new board for resentence and let this board of review decide upon the sentence, then we've still got a new bunch of officers deciding how much time he could get. But the reason that argument is of no avail, because if it went back, he would have two more steps of commutation, which he has lost, which is a substantive right in this case. The entire issue between you is whether or not the board of review or a new court mark will reset the sentence? Yes, sir. Whether or not that board of review under this particular set of circumstances had the authority to issue a sentence in this case. If the matter had been sent back to a new court marshal, would new evidence be introducible on the question of sentence? I believe on the question of character and appropriateness of sentence that would have been. On the issue of guilt, I don't believe so. Well, on the issue of sentence, was there any difference as far as the availability of evidence on the mitigating circumstances as between sending it back to the new court marshal or having the board of review do it? Would the board of review do the same thing? The board of review could, your honor, except for this one thing. It loses the defendant his right for two clemency appeals. appeals. And that's where we run into the difficulty. If there were still two more clemency appeals, then we would have a good situation. Now, go ahead. The government in their brief, for the first time since the solicitor general's office has it, says that the board of review actually has the power, the way I read it, to impose this sentence. Now, when Colonel Cordes of the Army was arguing with me about the case, the Army maintained this board of review never had the power to impose a sentence, and nobody in the Army feels like they have the power to impose a sentence, that they only remitted the sentence. But it was one of those cases, we cut a pie in half, which half you're going to have, this half or that half? As a matter of fact, under these circumstances, they did impose a sentence, because the original trial court did not have any discretionary powers in determining what the sentence ought to be. Now, the board of review could look at it and approve it, or they could say, this man has been in prison already for six years, we think that's enough time for him to have served under this kind, we cut it to time served. They wouldn't have the authority to raise it under any circumstances. cases. Now, in trial court, when Judge Hooper decided this case in our favor, I believe he decided it on the basis of one question he asked Colonel Cordes and Captain Smith of the Army. He said, Colonel and Captain, can either of you gentlemen tell me how much sentence that original court marshal would have given this man had he been found not guilty of murder, as the board of review said he should have been, and both of them says, we don't know, the record don't disclose it, and that's the same position we're in right now. They might have given him 20 years, I grant you. They might not have given him anything, but we don't know, and the board of review didn't know. Mr. Epstein, your argument would greatly impress me at least, but for one fact, but for one consideration. it would greatly impress me if, should you prevail here, the duty of resentencing would have to be exercised by the people who heard the evidence and make an assessment on the defendant, the kind of a fellow he was, the testimony he gets to. But, as I understand this, you can correct me if I'm wrong, as I understand it, the resentence, the retrial, as it's called, of the sentence, very accurate description, the reconsideration of the sentence would be by as different a body of men as the men that constitute the board of review. And, therefore, the chief consideration, when there is an improper or a doubtful sentence, that the persons who heard the merits should impose the sentence, because the sentence is to be individualized and grow out of that which they heard on the merit, fail here. And it seems to me substituting one group of non-participants in the trial for another group. Well, could I answer that, Your Honor, in saying this? It's not a failure on the part of our defender, but it's a failure on the part of the congressional and practice procedure in itself not to provide for it. Well, when you say failure, I do not understand that there is a constitutional challenge to the power of Congress to provide for a resentencing by a different body than here in the America. That is correct, isn't it? We have raised that issue. We've raised the issue that if Congress had let the Board of Review actually resentence the man, it would be unconstitutional. Are you raising that here? Yes, sir. It's in our original pleadings. And it, in other words, we were reversed. I believe we were limited to the gross sentence question, but I believe it grows out of it. I believe this court would hold it as repugnant to due process to let a man who is tried 5,000 miles away have his record be sent to Washington by a different board to decide how much time he is to serve. I know under the federal system of justice, if this same case would prevailed, it would have been sent back to the trial judge for resentence, and if the trial judge had died in the meantime to a new judge. If it were the federal system of justice to which you refer, you'd have to have jury trial and all the other requirements of the Bill of Rights. But this is military justice. with all the differentiation in treatment that the clause of the Constitution very carefully accepted by saying it shouldn't apply to military trial. And therefore the human, practical, reasonable consideration to which you refer and which I deeply share isn't constitutionally applicable to this situation. Because you're dealing with a military differentiation that is so controlling that the fathers were aware of it. In other words, you can't, you can send a case back to the same judge, because he's the same judge. But practically speaking, you can't send it back to the same court-martial, though in a particular case you could. Because they're scattered all over the world. If it please the court, I believe in the Burns case, in which you wrote a dissenting opinion, you raised those very questions as to whether or not a soldier has any rights under due process of law. And if they... I don't say you have none. I don't say you have none. But I'm saying this particular thing. I do not see, rightly enough, it isn't here, it was being raised before the Third Circuit, namely that it isn't, you've got a situation which practically, human, intrinsically, is so different in the case of military justice from the case of civil justice that it's impossible to send it back to the same trial. But if it please the court, if it is impossible, why does the procedure have to be such that it has to be sent back? In other words, it is a procedure that requires that it has to be sent back for justice if it's impossible, have to be followed if an alternate procedure would be available. I'm not suggesting that the consideration that I put to you destroys your case. I'm suggesting the argument you make as lacks a powerful appeal that controls civil justice. I thought your point was that you want the title of the code to a hearing on sentencing. We feel like, yes, under the code, it could be sent back to a fresh court-martial for the purposes of re-sentence. But you've had a hearing before the Board of Review. But you didn't have a hearing on sentencing before that board, did you? No, sir. In other words, when the Board of Review... That is your complaint. Your complaint isn't that the Board of Review often acted arbitrarily. Your complaint is that they have no power and it must be sent back to an ad hoc court-martial. That in this particular case, when they issued a sentence, that sentence was void in that it was not contained in the original sentence, and if it was, they had no way of knowing. In other words, under a gross sentence rules, a gross sentence can be divided if divisible. Now, if divisible is a key word. Was this sentence divisible? Was there any way in creation to know that it was divisible without going back? Now, if it was not divisible, why couldn't it be sent back to a court-martial and give these two defendants their two rights of clemency as we are asking? In other words, if it goes back to an original court-martial, we can make a plea for anything we want to in there. Will your client debarred from arguing before the Board of Review after the murder charge was knocked out? Will you debarred from arguing with that tribunal, the Board of Review, what sentence less than the maximum they should impose? If it pleased the court, I could say this about the Board of Review. In a murder conviction, that's automatic. Counsel is appointed by the Army to defend the man. He's paid by the Army to defend him. Automatically, they pick up the record and they go through with it. This man, as a matter of fact, says nothing to the Board of Review. He only reads the results. He's never given an opportunity to face the Board of Review and says, I've been a good soldier. I've been in the Army for six years and I've never been... He's not represented before the Board? His attorney presents the case before him, who is an Army attorney, but the man himself has no opportunity to show his character. His cause, it is... Has his cause, under sentence, a hearing before the Board? Yes, it's mandatory. I'm not suggesting that any of these questions imply my conclusion. I don't know what the facts are. It's mandatory under the statute. That he be represented. That he be represented. And that his claim for reduction in the sentence be represented. If the counsel thinks... Yes, sir. So that the hearing is not a hearing in abstracto, but you want a hearing before a newly constituted court marshal. Yes, sir. We want those other two rights that he didn't have.
